chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
title: Don Redman as an exacting, gentlemanly arranger
summary: Don Redman graduated in music, played ocarina, led a band that drove Sidney DeParis's lips hard, and was always a gentleman.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah, but, you know, first time I came here in '37 Willie Bryant had a (unintelligible) that band at the Savoy. So my wife knew him, I think. Anyway, he came over and sat talking to us, that -- I said, who's playing that good trumpet solo there. He said, Sidney DeParis. I said, well, what's he doing in your band? He said, oh, he's very glad to be in my band. He said, he's just got out of Don Redman's band, and he said that was tearing his lips to pieces. So, he said, my band is much easier for him.
Yes, he was. He finished that Virginia State University. He finished down there in music, you know, and he could play -- I think the ocarina was a little, funny instrument.
Oh, he used to play that?
Yeah, he used to feature it. It got so he recorded with Fletcher on that thing.
Well, I first thought Don was his vocals. They were funny. I think they were very funny. Do you remember that one, 'Try and Get a Good Night's Sleep?'
Right. I tell you the one I liked was his theme, though, for his band was 'Chant of the Weeds.'
Oh, well, that was -- now, that is -- I mean that's -- Duke said that was about the heaviest competition they ever got.
Pity he didn't do more work like that because he obviously could have done it. I guess Don was, you know -- I mean he did a lot of work, but in a sense he was an easygoing man.
You know, Duke he was a hustler, really.
Yeah, very nice, always a gentleman.
He -- I mean I didn't know him that well, but he -- you'd think you were a long lost friend or something, the way he'd speak to you.
